items.stem: Which of the following is true regarding leftist political groups in the 1960s?
options: (A) Their leadership tended to be female dominated in keeping with feminist ideals.
(B) They were sharply divided in terms of those who supported the Vietnam War and those who opposed it.
(C) They were fiercely opposed to the Warren Court on ideological grounds.
(D) They caused a conservative backlash in the 1970s.
items.explanation: The radical leftist politics of the 1960s caused a conservative reaction in the 1970s, with the formation of many groups that advocated for a return to traditional American values on issues such as abortion, affirmative action, sexual morality, etc. However, leftist political groups in the 1960s were unified in their opposition to the Vietnam War and were ideologically aligned with the highly liberal Supreme Court under Earl Warren (although some believed the Court did not push the liberal agenda hard enough). While some groups took a strong feminist stance, most remained male-dominated, with women serving in supporting roles.

option_explanations.A: Despite feminist rhetoric, most 1960s leftist groups remained male-dominated in their leadership.
option_explanations.B: The 1960s left was unified in opposing the Vietnam War, not split between supporters and opponents of it.
option_explanations.C: The left was ideologically aligned with Earl Warren's liberal Supreme Court, not opposed to it — though some felt the Court did not go far enough.
option_explanations.D: The radicalism of the 1960s provoked a conservative backlash in the 1970s, with new organizations pushing a return to traditional values on abortion, affirmative action, and sexual morality.

items.stem: Which of the following does NOT accurately describe the presidential election of 1968?
options: (A) The Democratic Party was fractured because of dissent over the Vietnam War.
(B) A frontrunner for one of the major parties was assassinated during the primary season.
(C) Both major-party candidates campaigned as Washington outsiders.
(D) A third-party candidacy split the traditionally Democratic southern vote.
items.explanation: The Republican candidate, Richard Nixon, was a former vice president. The Democratic candidate, Hubert Humphrey, was the current vice president and, before that, a longtime senator. Neither could have campaigned as a Washington outsider, and neither did. The Democrats were fractured over the war; the party was home to both aggressive cold warriors and the antiwar movement. Robert Kennedy was assassinated in June; many believe he would have won the nomination had he not been killed. George Wallace formed a third party and campaigned on states’ rights and segregation, siphoning off key votes in the South, where the Democrats had traditionally done well. Nixon’s only opposition in the Republican primaries came from Nelson D. Rockefeller, who campaigned halfheartedly, and Ronald Reagan, who, at the time, was seen as too extreme to ever win the presidency. Reagan never changed, but the country did.

option_explanations.A: The Democrats were genuinely fractured over Vietnam — the 1968 Chicago convention dissolved into chaos between cold warriors and the antiwar movement. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Robert Kennedy was genuinely assassinated in June 1968 during the primaries, when many believed he would win the nomination. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Neither major-party candidate could plausibly run as a Washington outsider: Nixon was a former vice president and Humphrey was the sitting vice president and a longtime senator. This does not accurately describe the election — it is the exception.
option_explanations.D: George Wallace genuinely ran a third-party campaign on states' rights and segregation that split the traditionally Democratic southern vote. This accurately describes the election, so it is not the exception.

items.stem: Inflation throughout the 1970s was driven in large part by
options: (A) the cost of funding the Vietnam War
(B) rapidly increasing gasoline and oil prices
(C) government investment in the space program
(D) a dramatic reduction of income tax rates
items.explanation: Gasoline and oil prices shot through the roof in the 1970s, affecting a wide range of industries that relied on the fuels to run. The result was widespread inflation throughout the decade.

option_explanations.A: Vietnam War spending fed inflation in the late 1960s, but the 1970s inflation was driven by something else: the decade's defining shocks were energy shocks, not war spending.
option_explanations.B: The OPEC oil embargo (1973) and the 1979 energy crisis sent gasoline and oil prices soaring. Since fuel costs run through nearly every industry, the result was the decade's grinding stagflation.
option_explanations.C: Space-program spending peaked with Apollo in the 1960s. It was not the driver of 1970s inflation.
option_explanations.D: There was no dramatic income-tax cut in the 1970s — the big rate cuts came under Reagan in 1981. Tax policy did not drive the decade's inflation.
